description:
Sponsor: Montech HyperFlow 360 Cooler on Amazon https://geni.us/dWBIbF6
The AMD Radeon RX 9070 video card is shipping alongside the RX 9070 XT and surprised us with its efficiency. The power-to-performance ratio is strong on the RX 9070 non-XT, seemingly finding a "sweet spot" of balance between power consumption and the output. The 9070 and 9070 XT are known to have a weirdly small $50 gap between them, at an MSRP of $550 and $600, but in either case, the two have ganged-up on the NVIDIA RTX 5070 GPU to effectively invalidate its existence -- even more than NVIDIA already did. This review benchmarks the performance of the RX 9070 vs. the 9070 XT, RTX 5070, RX 6700 XT, 6600, and plenty more.

comments.text: Thanks for all these reviews and the intensive work it must have taken!  I've noted GN have started using 'swing' to mean 'improvement' or 'difference' in the last few videos.  Is this being used normally?  As I've only heard of swing used in electoral swing, where is does not mean the raw difference, but the (assumed) transfer from A to B.  e.g. A and B both have 40% one time, then next time A has 35% and B has 45% - that's a 5% swing resulting in a 10% difference in share.  But here, we're not transferring performance from one GPU to another; it's just a difference.

comments.text:
I crunched the numbers this entire morning spending time comparing 9070 vs 9070 xt with same settings, the xt has lower W/fps than non-xt (i.e. better efficiency) when it's at -30% PL vs non-xt stock or even optimized with undervolt for same W in the range of: 220-250W, in other words, it has higher fps for same W vs non-xt, but that range ~30W is very small and near the limit of -30% PL. Why did NOBODY talk about this and test this? The 9070 is NOT ALWAYS defacto better efficiency vs the xt from my tests with hard data, only when it's out of xt's range. For shit and giggles, apples to apples: non-xt also with -30% PL, it is +22% more efficient and when both are maxed overclocked (again, same settings) it's 27% more efficient and the max overclock is barely less efficient than stock or optimized... so you either take the extreme -30% PL OR +10% PL max overclock for the best results for the non-xt, there is no in between like with nvidia where you can manually set a V/MHz curve to makes it worthwhile.

The xt is good for -30% PL (still faster and more efficient than optimized non xt at stock W) OR when you need more power than non-xt max overclock, but the W/fps goes exponential (i.e. way less efficient) the higher you go. The max overclock I could reach with 9070 asus tuf is +12.5%, which did NOT beat the xt at stock (test is warhammer 3, a proper full raster gpu hammering game, so perfect for testing the raw power and the only graphical intensive game I play).

This choice is for you to make. I choose the 9070 for efficiency (settings used and that I apply, fully stable: -30% PL -60mv fast timings) which is low power consumption, so low heat and therefore low noise with plenty of power leftover and by the time max overclock is not enough (+10% PL -60mv +200mhz core fasting timings), then I will upgrade. I could have bought the xt tuf for 10% more, but decided against it, for my own reasons I've just said. For +15% more performance inc max overclock xt, on 4k wh3 ultra and extreme shadows, it would have gone to 4.19W/fps (max overclock xt) vs 3.29W/fps (max overclock non-xt, same settings) => +27.36% W needed for same fps, by that time, we are on <= 3nm nodes and gddr7.

Hope this helps. Don't feel bad buying the 9070, it could be the better choice, depending on your needs. If you don't give a shit about power consumption and noise and price is also within 10% range, then definitely buy the xt.
comments.author: @mrzeus9411

comments.text: I did more research and locked to same fps (either vsync or hard cap) and xt is IDENTICAL to non xt perf/W. Reviewers are full of shit when they compare apples with oranges, i.e. stock 300W vs 220W, ofc the higher end spectrum, that on the xt is less efficient, but for same W, they're identical fps/W... I didn't knew this, coming from nvidia (last amd card was r9 290x 11 years ago), because nvidia is completely different where you can manually tune each voltage point with different mhz. Amd undervolting and power limits work completely different on a curve offset, which is identical for both xt and non xt... the power limit does not affect efficiency at all... it only sets the limit how more W can be used, so the internal curve that you can NOT change and is hidden from view is still the same and ALWAYS more efficient on the lower voltage range than higher. Time for reviewers to do a proper apples-to-apples comparison, show the efficiency for the same W and they would be identical, misleading conclusions that non xt is more efficient than xt are HIGHLY MISLEADING. Only on stock settings, but you compare apples-to-oranges to begin with. Then it can be concluded that xt is always is best when <= $/fps as fps/W <= non xt is IDENTICAL and it has additional 3rd 8-pin pcie connector to catch transient power spikes and additional vrms (at least on asus tuf). comments.text:
Genuine question here.  I see your reviews focus on the average FPS.  But in reality, isn't the 1% lows more important?  The closer the 1% low is to the average FPS, the more smooth the gameplay is.  A 1% low (and 0.1% low) that is further away from the average FPS indicates times where the GPU was unable to maintain a consistent FPS.

In other words, you could have a couple scenes that were easy and the card just rips right through them, skewing to a high(er) average FPS, but bogs down in other scenes -- indicated by the 1% and 0.1% lows.

Now.  On the 9070 and 9070 XT.  You seem to be focusing exclusively on average FPS, and in the case of the 9070, since the average FPS of the 9070 is higher than the 5070, we all seem to be ringing the bell for AMD.

However.

If you calculate out the 1% low and the 0.1% low percentage drops for both the 9070 and the 5070, you'll notice something interesting.  Using your Dragon's Dogma 2 4K chart as the example, the 9070 drops 18.5% of its fps in the 1% low, and 21.4% in the 0.1% low.

By comparison, the 5070 drops 17.3% for 1%, and only 18.5% for 0.1%.  In other words, the 5070 is dropping the equivalent fps at 0.1% as the 9070 is at 1%.  Doesn't this indicate that the 5070, despite having a lower average FPS, would actually provide a better, smoother gaming experience with less stuttering and fewer frame drops?

For future reviews, I don't think it's sufficient to just report on average FPS as that doesn't really tell the entire story.  There is significance in the 1% drops.  I understand that you are frustrated with Nvidia's marketing bullshit -- trust me when I say you aren't the only one; however, we should still strive to be objective in our analysis of real-world GPU performance.  I'm not saying you aren't, but I am saying I think critical pieces of information aren't being emphasized enough in the analysis.

Should it surprise anyone that when you get into the sweet spot of the efficiency curve of a particular process node that products will be very efficient?

Both AMD and Nvidia are using TSMC N4, the 9070 is clocked slower than the 9070 XT so I would ASSUME it would be more efficient though that's not what I'm looking for personally.  It's a bigger deal under normal usage but when gaming I want to push the GPU unless the GPU is already giving me what I want and then I might cap frame rates to slow it down and save energy but I'll push it if it's not giving me the fps I want, and I'm not picky.  In open world games I want 1% lows to be above 60 fps as that's smooth enough game play for me.

Of course the 9070 XT isn't going to be the most efficient since it's a top end product for AMD and the die they're using and the clocks are above that sweet spot.  Of course one can limit the max clock rate and make it more efficient and it will still be better than the 9070 due to more cores.

comments.text:
I have noticed that different boards at different price points from different board partners differ in quality and features. For example, high priced cards usually have higher quality coolers that cool better with less noise. Lower priced cards could have corners cut from the cooler like not having their fins soldered to the heat pipes, lowering costs and heat transfer from the heat pipes to the cooling fins. Lower priced cards could also use fans with bad quality bearings such as sleeve bearings to cut corners.

Higher priced cards tend to have better voltage regulator modules which produce better regulated power for the GPU which allows it to run at higher clocks and generate less severe power spikes that your power supply unit has to absorb and compensate for, limiting wear and tear to the power supply unit. Should the spikes be too large for the PSU to absorb, the parts of the power spikes that the PSU failed to absorb could also accelerate wear and tear to other parts that are connected to the same power rail as the graphics card.

Also, better board partners add safety and reliability features like fuses or structural reinforcement. Should a short circuit develop on the video card and blow a fuse, the fuse prevents the short circuit from further damaging the video card and allows the video card to be successfully repaired instead of getting totaled by the damage that the short circuit could have caused. Many lower quality video cards lack fuses. Higher priced cards sometimes add structural reinforcement to allow cards to withstand more stress before the stress damages or wears out the video cards. Higher priced video cards could also add more card monitoring features like thermometers or power monitoring shunt resistors.

comments.text:
I honestly thought the RX 9070 would pull further ahead of the RTX 5070. This is bad for AMD, although I still feel a $500 price point would make more sense for both cards.

The reasons I believe this is really bad for AMD are because while in spitting distance of each other in raster, the RTX 5070 clearly has the higher RT compute budget (with the RX 9070 only ever pulling ahead in games it doesn't exceed that budget & holds a raster advantage in already)...

Plus, the transformer model DLSS4 uses is generationally superior to FSR4. Am I missing anything?.... Oh yeah! "RTX 4090 performance", or MFG! 240 Hz+ panels will be flying off shelves now. 😶‍🌫

I really don't want the tech reviewer space to become this huge echo chamber totally disconnected from the gaming experience. It's disheartening, to say the least. I do understand the cynicism anyway. Nvidia isn't what I'd call pro consumer, but AMD isn't what I'd call innovative either. 

I like that AMD is going in the right direction anyways, but comparing and contrasting the 9070 XT and RTX 5070 Ti (ignoring the price), which have similar die sizes and raster performance, but hugely different power envelopes & feature sets really exposes the architectural differences. AMD cannot make a RTX 5090 competitor. It'd be a space heater without any of the RTX goodness. This marketing about targeting a segment is total hogwash. This simply is where AMD's architecture sits in 2025.

comments.text:
At this point I really do think AMD should bring back Crossfire 'AND' fix all the issues it had. Crossfire/SLI absolutely disrupts product segmentation, and this time around AMD does not have a high end offering. However if you could purchase a $1200 card that has higher performance then a 5090 they would sell out like hotcakes. It's one of the reasons that CF/SLI was never improved upon, AMD/Nvidia were basically fighting against themselves. You have to spend R&D on technology that not only ruins your current product segmentation, but also makes old cards that would be antiquated gain new life, possibly for a lot longer.

However, times have changed at this point and AMD doesn't have a high end, nor did they have an extreme high end with the last generation. Crossfire very much could give them a huge lead. With PCIE4/5 latency and bandwidth wouldn't even be a concern as well and there are plenty of people who would go for 2x9070XTs for roughly half the cost of a 5090... if you can even find a non-scalped card.

It really would be sliding a spear in a spot Nvidia would have to address. While AMD can't really win RT performance, while trying, they can definitely win in value and rasterization if they tried. It's entirely possible for them to fix all the issues that were never addressed with CF/SLI as well, especially now days after further refining optimizations for games and frame times being better understood.

comments.text:
As a 4070TI owner who will be probably until 6000 series or beyond - I don't upgrade until I see serious gameplay degradation or get a really good deal - I'm happy for the AMD fanboys. Not because of pricing, blah blah BS every reviewer focuses on (we're PC builders, if we were really that cost focused we would have bought a console) but because these are actually decent products.

Assuming the upscaling isn't garbage (and I'll assume they worked as hard on that as they did on finally creating a viable RT card), they finally have a product that holds its own not only in rasterization, but also can hold its own in RT at a reasonable price and wins its bracket comfortably without the usual caveats or creative narrative that you have to throw in to keep AMD in the game. That's a huge win.

Now will it win them market share? I don't think so. It's a win for the DIY community, but system integrators are where the war is fought, and they don't pay online pricing. For them, who won't be having to choose between a $900 5070 and a $550 9070 but rather will be paying about the same? They'll still go Nvidia because it's the guaranteed sale. The pricing is still too high for the demand of the product. You've got a legitimate winner here, but it's neck and neck with the market leader on price, for market share, not DIY, they needed this to be probably a $400 card at launch, not in a year when it will definitely be a $400 card. (Edit: Unless we actually see the GPU shortages being forecasted, then it'll be 2021 all over again and this will be a $700 card or some crazy nonsense)

comments.text:
Hi Steve & the Gamers Nexus crew!  I don't often comment on videos as a general rule but after watching I wanted to say a few things.
First off: Thank-you, this was a great selection of data to peruse and I really appreciate you placing Turing & particularly the 2070, Super (which I sadly own) and the 2080/Ti in the benchmarks and even at 4k! This is something I can appreciate as someone who uses both integer scaling @ 1440p on a 4k display and on these cards. It was a very nice surprise to see this data represented and also hits into that sweet spot you were talking about in the intro.
I thank-you for continuing to keep things like this around as someone who builds a PC, upgrades or slots in components over the years may have had a performance class card that's toughed it out for 4 or 5 years. The Turing refresh cards are only 4.5~ years old. Great work in including that and it was nice to see cards that matched in TDP or were within a ball hair.

Secondly: That sweet spot. You've really tapped into what the 9070 offers and can offer someone like myself. I care about TDP, power consumption and I have a Turing card that's long in the tooth. I grumbled a bit back in 2018 & 2019 when the TDP was raised and avoided both Ampere, Ada and RDNA because they offered cards at either a similar TDP or much higher while not offering much in the ways of a performance uplift. RDNA3 got close but I had DLSS available at the time for some titles and the pricing didn't really work out until RDNA4 was approaching so it was worth holding off. I thank-you for continuing to keep things like this around.
I looked on your site and couldn't see a full review but I'd love to see one with things like PPW with the Turing cards and even the RDNA cards in the same power envelope!
-and speaking of power envelopes. It was nice to see you mention them and the lower end of the scale, you mentioned runaway pricing. For someone concerned about energy use, runaway power is one too!

Closing up. This review was great, I didn't have to pause too much and if I did it was to look at the numbers. You seemed to have a good grasp of how it compared vs RDNA3 and the generational uplift. On another channel I had to constantly pause the videos, run the numbers myself to check the uplift and it appeared they were very performance focused. So a massive thank-you to everyone on the team who made this possible: I hope you all get some much deserved rest.

I would love to see a video in the future surrounding discussions on power consumption/tdp maybe with undervolting guides/OCing on AMD, Intel and even Nvidia.
Really again, thank-you and I hope you all have a very pleasant year!

comments.text:
@joeykeilholz925  what's the power draw of the undervolted 5090?

Edit: Initially I did not bother calculating it with exact numbers just rough stuff in my head, but now that I did the numbers are absurd. 
A decent B rated 380 - 400 litre fridge-freezer would consume ~220kwh/ year.

A 5090 with a TDP of 575w used 4 hours a day lets say draws 500w. That would be 730 kwh / year if using the 500w.

So just the the GPU will draw 3.34 times more power than a 400L fridge-freezer that's not even the most efficient power rating. That's without adding in a CPU, case fans, motherboard etc.

Ofc if you buy a 5090 and game on a 4k monitor maybe you don't care about those numbers but even if you use the RX 9070 220w TDP for 4 hours that gives you 321.2 kWh/ year still 100 kwh more than a 400l fridge freezer. That's how bad the efficiency effort is.

comments.text:
@ArtisChronicles  Undervolting reduces power draw, so lower power is needed for the same frequency. But modern CPUs cap their frequency based on power draw, so if you are using 10% less power to maintain 5GHz let's say, instead of just using 10% less power, the CPU automatically just increases frequency say 5% so you still will be at the power limit.

Basically frequency isn't set in stone like it was 10+ years ago, CPUs have power and thermal limit set, and if you are below those and under load, the CPU will speed itself up until it hits a limit. This is why CPU frequencies tends to be listed as "up to". Also, different loads draw different power, so some loads may be fine running 5.5 Ghz, while others taxing SIMD units may drop to 5 GHz or lower for same power.

CPUs and GPUs ship stock with very conservative voltage settings so come hell or high water, it will be stable which is most important. Most the time, and for most workloads you can reduce voltage at least slightly and maintain stability. Typically you undervolt until you get instability, then increase voltage somewhat to maintain stability, and maybe a bit more for peace of mind.

The higher up the voltage curve you go, you get diminishing returns. This is why laptops can be somewhat comparable to desktop performance but draw significantly less power. You may bet 60% the performance at 25% the power.
comments.author: @xeridea

comments.text: @ArtisChronicles  That happens because by dropping voltage, you are also dropping heat, and that can allow the chip to clock faster because it's not thermally constraint. Naturally, that won't be ALWAYS the case, but it isn't too crazy because as cards are mass produced, they have to account for the lower quality yields and keeping them stable. So if you win (or stay on the upper half) the silicon lottery, you will certainly see benefits for no downsides by undervolting.

comments.text: @DeanTheLaughingMann  Well, before ATX 3.x, you could only "outdo" GPU power spikes (up to 600 W in case of the XT) with pure wattage, whereas the new standard requires PSUs to be able to handle spikes of up to 200% of their rating; high-quality 750 W ATX 3.1 should be enough for the XT - 850 W if you own a thirsty Intel (e.g. 14700K has a gaming-average of 150 W vs. the 7800X3D's mind-blowingly low 50!).
comments.author: @rockapartie

comments.text: @thiscouldntblowmore  The problem with PSU recommendations are the power spikes: In case of the XT, they can go as high as 500 W (worst-case 600 W in stress tests). In the past, PSUs weren't guaranteed to be able to handle them, unless their wattage far exceeded what your PC actually consumed under 100% load; since ATX 3.x, PSUs must be able to handle millisecond-spikes of up to 200% of their rating, therefore, 750 W ATX 3.1 from a decent manufacturer should be more than enough for the 9070 XT.

@TooBokoo actually you can and should hold Nvidia accountable for the scalpers.

They know it's a thing in the industry. Despite that, they decided to rush out a launch with basically no stock and the little stock they had exhibiting manufacturing defects just prior to an expected, major factory shutdown in China, where most of the cards are produced.

All in order to get some exposure (that they didn't need, they are Nvida) during some January conventions, to pre-empt AMD and to lock in a lower MSRP before the announced Trump administration tariffs.

In other words, their MSRP was a deliberate  lie from the very beginning and then they severely exacerbated the issue by having so little stock that it pretty much guaranteed being fully snatched up by scalpers.

I'm tired of pretending companies shouldn't be held accountable for their deliberately bad decisions. There are ways to deal with scalping. You can make purchasing limit contracts. You can release with sufficient stock. You can ensure that production is ready to go so people don't expect to wait months to years for a chance at your product.

This is in the same vein as defending AAA publishers for selling games piece-meal and pushing their release before they are finished just because others are doing it.

comments.text:
The raw BOM cost of the 9070XT is basically no more than the BOM cost of the 7800XT which had an MSRP of $499 and regularly sold for $450. Sure I get that 4nm is ever so slightly more expensive than 5nm but at the same time GDDR6 prices have come down, other costs like shipping and general inflation might have also increased but I think AMD could have been more aggressive if they really really wanted to, but $599 in the current climate of basically 'no competition from Nvidia' is good enough and will sell very well. The 5070Ti is certainly not worth $300-400 more than the 9070XT, but AMD needs to be really careful because if Nvidia sorts themselves out (this could happen if it's yield issues or something else we don't know) and start to fill shelves with $749 cards then 100% AMD can not look to charge $650-700+ for this card which has been rumoured once all the MSRP cards are sold. 
The 5070Ti is better in every single way, but it's just not '$300 better', but most buyers including myself would happy pay $50-100 more for better overall performance, better power usage, better ray tracing, better and wider DLSS support, Reflex, HDR, better encoding quality, better support in content creation apps, Cuda, the list goes on. I genuinely had my heart set on a 5070Ti this year (I've not owned Nvidia in about 20 years!) but the performance increase wasn't that impressive and the pricing/available is just ridiculous. Thankfully AMD looks to have got their sh!t together this generation, it's a solid card, decent performance, they are addressing their shortcomings and they have currently priced this card where it needs to be in the market we have right now. But honestly, AMD can't go north of $600 long term as this card simply isn't good enough against a $749 5070Ti, imo.

comments.text:
@Varonth  That doesn't sound like AMD lied about the price, but rather weren't strict enough with retailers/3rd party vendors with pricing agreements to try stop companies between AMD and the products hitting the shelves from trying to exploit the situation and rip people off.

If prices are now going up after the initial stock sold out and retailers/3rd party card manufacturers were only held to a certain price for the first shipment, then the reason the price is going up is because of the retailers greed and wanting to take advantage of people.

Not because of AMD.

That said, I doubt AMD really had much direct contact with retailers over these cards, given all of them are 3rd party vendor cards.

AMD supply the chips at a certain price to the 3rd party vendors to manufacture their cards. The 3rd party vendors then work out pricing deals with retailers for their cards.

So my money is on either retailers are hiking the prices, or 3rd party vendors are pushing for higher prices after seeing that the cards will sell, and they want to exploit their customers for as much as possible picking up lessons from papa Jensen.
